subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Contrast Effect
description: A micro-lesson that makes Contrast Effect usable.

hook.text: A $200 shirt seems expensive. Place it beside a $2,000 suit and suddenly it feels like a bargain.

buildup.text: The contrast effect: our perception of something changes depending on what we compare it to. Context shifts value.

discovery.text: Real estate agents show a terrible house first. The next house looks amazing by contrast, even if it is average.

twist.text: Salary negotiations use this. A high first offer makes a moderate counter-offer feel like a concession.

climax.text: Judge every option on its own merits, not relative to what came before. Comparisons are chosen to manipulate you.

punchline.text: What something sits next to changes what it looks like.

quiz.question: Why do real estate agents show a bad house first?
options: To test if buyers are paying attention
To make the next house look better by contrast
Because bad houses are easier to sell

details.summary: The contrast effect distorts judgment by making options seem better or worse depending on what they are compared to. A mediocre option looks great after a terrible one, and an excellent option looks ordinary after an exceptional one.
details.whyItMatters: The contrast effect is exploited in sales, negotiation, and presentation order. A real estate agent shows a terrible house first to make the next one seem wonderful.
takeaways: Judgments are heavily influenced by what was seen immediately before
A bad option makes a mediocre option seem good by comparison
Savvy sellers engineer contrast by controlling the sequence of options shown

faq.question: How is the contrast effect used in sales?
faq.answer: Salespeople show the most expensive option first, making the target item seem reasonably priced by contrast. Real estate agents show an overpriced property first. Negotiators make an extreme initial offer to make their real ask seem reasonable.

faq.question: How can you protect yourself from the contrast effect?
faq.answer: Evaluate each option against your pre-defined criteria rather than against the previous option. Set your standards before seeing any options. Avoid making decisions immediately after exposure to an extreme comparison point.
